newsitem.title: USA: Red Cross Holocaust papers tarnish its image - paper.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross Holocaust papers tarnish its image - paper.

text.p: Documents that go on public display in the United States on Friday paint an unflattering picture of the failure of the International Committee of the Red Cross to take action against the Holocaust, the USA Today newspaper said.

The documents helped show "how not just governments but international organisations reneged on their human responsibility in the face of Nazi horror," the newspaper quoted American University history professor Alan Kraut.

The newspaper said it had early access to nearly 25,000 documents available for public viewing at Washington's U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum. The ICRC made all their reports public in Geneva around two months ago, it said.

International Red Cross chief spokesman in Geneva, Kim Gordon-Bates, was quoted as saying: "We were inefficient, undoubtedly, in Nazi Germany." But he said the Red Cross was not alone in this respect.

Documents showed that when ICRC officials visited Auschwitz in 1944 to sanitize parts of the concentration camp, they wrote that a camp prisoner told them of "a very modern shower room in the concentration camp where the internees are reportedly gassed in large groups...But it was impossible to prove anything," USA Today said, quoting documents.

In a subsequent letter to U.S. State Department officials about the visit, the ICRC was quoted by USA Today as saying: "(We) had not been able to discover any trace of installations for exterminating civilian prisoners. (This) corroborates a report which we have already received from other sources, ie that for several months there had been no further exterminations at Auschwitz."

USA Today said Red Cross workers wrote after an August 14, 1940 visit to Buchenwald concentration camp that the facility, complete with a prison library, was clean and that inmates appeared healthy and well-treated.

"All the buildings are surrounded by flower beds and grass...giving the camp a happy note," the Red Cross report was quoted as saying. "It is evident the most modern means are being used for the treatment of...prisoners." The paper said the illusion was deliberately prepared by the Nazis.
But the paper said some of the documents did show the ICRC in a good light, struggling to cope with an unprecedented humanitarian crisis.
They showed the international ICRC delivered 1.6 million relief parcels behind Axis lines during the Second World War.
USA Today said many Jewish leaders and Holocaust experts had long maintained the ICRC failed during the war by not raising alarm about atrocities.

In 1995, the ICRC, which coordinates Red Cross relief to civilians in wartime and enforces the Geneva convention of the treatment of prisoners, acknowledged for the first time its "moral failure" during the war -- a reference to its failure to denounce atrocities against Jews and other minorities in Hitler's concentration camps.

Last August, the World Jewish Congress highlighted U.S. intelligence documents uncovered in the U.S. National Archives that alleged that some ICRC representatives worked as agents for German intelligence, conveying military information to Berlin, and that Red Cross pouches were used to ferry German assets into Switzerland.
